questions.stem: Which type of network covers the smallest area, such as one laboratory or one building?
questions.explanation: A Local Area Network (LAN) joins computers within a small area such as a room, a building or a campus. A MAN spreads over a city, a WAN over countries and the Internet over the whole world.

optionRationale.1: A MAN covers a whole city, which is much larger than a building.
optionRationale.2: A WAN covers countries or continents.
optionRationale.3: The Internet is a worldwide network of networks, the largest of all.

questions.objective: Identify a LAN by its area

questions.stem: Which guided transmission medium has a central copper conductor surrounded by an insulator and a metal shield?
questions.explanation: A coaxial cable has a central copper conductor, an insulating layer, a metal shield and an outer cover, which is the design the question describes. Optical fibre carries light in glass, twisted pair uses twisted wire pairs, and a microwave link needs no cable at all.

optionRationale.1: Optical fibre has a glass or plastic core that carries light, not a copper conductor.
optionRationale.2: Twisted pair has pairs of insulated wires twisted together, without a central conductor and shield of this kind.
optionRationale.4: A microwave link is an unguided medium that uses radio waves through the air, not a cable.

questions.objective: Recognise the structure of a coaxial cable

questions.stem: Which hardware component is fitted inside a computer so that it can connect to a LAN?
questions.explanation: The Network Interface Card, also called the network adapter, is the part inside the computer that provides the connection to the network and carries the MAC address. A repeater, a switch and a gateway are separate network devices.

optionRationale.1: A repeater is a separate device placed on a cable to boost the signal.
optionRationale.2: A switch is an external device that joins many computers.
optionRationale.3: A gateway is a network device linking different networks, not a card fitted in a computer.

questions.objective: Recall the role of a NIC

questions.stem: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long. How many different IPv4 addresses are possible in all?
questions.explanation: Each of the 32 bits can be 0 or 1, so the number of different addresses is 2 raised to 32, which is 4,294,967,296. This is the same as 256^4, because the four decimal numbers each have 256 possible values.

optionRationale.1: 2^16 is the number of values of a 16-bit quantity, but the address has 32 bits.
optionRationale.3: 32^2 treats the number of bits as the base; each bit has two possible values, so the count is 2^32.
optionRationale.4: The address has four numbers of 0 to 255, so the count is 256^4, which is 2^32.

questions.objective: Compute the size of the IPv4 address space

questions.stem: A company links its branch offices in Delhi, Chennai and London with leased lines so that all of them share one network. Which type of network is this?
questions.explanation: The offices are separated by long distances across cities and countries, so the connected network spreads over a wide geographical area. Such a network is a Wide Area Network (WAN), and the Internet is the best known example.

optionRationale.2: A PAN is a small network around one person, usually within a few metres.
optionRationale.3: A LAN is limited to one building or campus, but these offices are in different cities and countries.
optionRationale.4: A MAN covers one city, but these offices are in different cities and countries.

questions.objective: Classify a network by its geographical spread

questions.stem: Match each network type in List-I with an example in List-II.
questions.explanation: A PAN covers the space around a person, so a phone with Bluetooth earphones is a PAN (I). A school laboratory is a LAN (II). A city-wide cable TV network is a MAN (III), and the Internet is the largest WAN (IV).

optionRationale.2: A PAN is around one person, such as a phone and earphones, and a LAN covers a lab; A and B are exchanged here.
optionRationale.3: A city-wide cable network is a MAN and the Internet is a WAN; C and D are exchanged here.
optionRationale.4: A school laboratory is a LAN and a city network is a MAN; B and C are exchanged here.

right: I. A phone connected to wireless earphones by Bluetooth
II. The computers of one school laboratory
III. A cable TV network spread over a city

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. A bus topology has a central switch to which every node is connected.
B. Wi-Fi uses radio waves to carry data.
C. Optical fibre carries data as pulses of light.
D. A MAN covers a larger area than a LAN.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A bus topology has one common backbone cable, not a central switch, so A is false. Wi-Fi sends data by radio waves (B true). Optical fibre sends data as pulses of light (C true). A MAN spreads over a city and so covers more area than a LAN (D true).

optionRationale.1: A is false: a bus topology uses a single backbone cable, whereas a star topology uses a central device.
optionRationale.2: A is false, and B and C are also correct.
optionRationale.4: C is also correct: light pulses travel through the glass fibre.

questions.objective: Judge statements about topologies, media and network types

questions.stem: How many more cables are needed to connect 12 computers in a full mesh than to connect them in a star topology (one cable from every computer to a central switch)?
questions.explanation: A full mesh of n computers needs n(n - 1)/2 cables, which is 12 x 11 / 2 = 66 for 12 computers. A star needs one cable per computer, so 12. The mesh needs 66 - 12 = 54 more cables.

optionRationale.1: 66 is the number of cables of the full mesh alone; the 12 cables of the star must be subtracted.
optionRationale.2: 12 is the number of cables of the star topology, not the difference.
optionRationale.3: 78 is 66 + 12, which adds the star cables to the mesh cables instead of subtracting them.

questions.objective: Compare cable counts of mesh and star

questions.stem: A school has three labs. Each lab is a star network of 5 computers connected to its own switch. The three switches are then joined in a ring (each switch connected to the next, the last to the first). How many cables are used in all?
questions.explanation: Each lab uses one cable per computer to its switch, which is 5 cables, so three labs use 15. A ring of three switches needs one cable between each neighbouring pair, which is 3 cables. The total is 15 + 3 = 18.

optionRationale.1: These are only the cables from the computers to their switches; the ring of the three switches adds more.
optionRationale.3: A ring of three switches needs 3 cables, one between each pair of neighbours, not 2.
optionRationale.4: The ring joins 3 switches, so it needs 3 cables; 6 would be too many.

questions.objective: Count cables in a hybrid topology

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A switch forwards a frame only to the port to which the destination computer is connected.
Reason (R): A switch is a network device that has many ports.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A switch learns the MAC address behind each port and sends a frame only to the port of the destination, so the assertion is true. The reason is also true, but having many ports does not explain this selective forwarding; the cause is its use of MAC addresses (a hub also has many ports but sends data to all).

optionRationale.1: Having many ports does not explain selective forwarding, since a hub also has many ports but still sends to all.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true: a switch has many ports.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: a switch sends a frame only to the destination port.

questions.objective: Judge whether a true reason explains switch behaviour
